docs.title: iceberg-loader
docs.text:
iceberg-loader wraps PyIceberg to load PyArrow data into Apache Iceberg tables. It handles mixed JSON fields, schema evolution, partition replacement, upserts, batches, and IPC streams.

Status: Actively developed and under testing. PRs are welcome! Tested against Hive Metastore and REST Catalog (Tabular, Polaris, self-hosted).

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Arrow-first: pa.Table, RecordBatch, IPC.
  • Messy JSON friendly: dict/list/mixed → JSON strings.
  • Schema evolution (opt-in).
  • Idempotent replace (replace_filter) and upsert.
  • Commit interval for long streams.
  • Maintenance helpers (expire snapshots).

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text: iceberg-loader-benchmark compares iceberg-loader with the dlt Iceberg destination. Both write the same Arrow data through a Polaris REST Catalog and MinIO. On a 1 GiB NYC 311 snapshot (1.72M rows), iceberg-loader had a median write time of 3.7 s and a median peak RSS of 1.36 GiB; dlt took 11.4 s and 2.26 GiB. The repo covers the methodology, raw data, and how to reproduce the run.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "iceberg-loader[all]"

Or with uv:

uv add "iceberg-loader[all]"

docs.title: Extras
docs.text: Extra Description hive Hive Metastore support s3 S3 filesystem support rest REST Catalog support (Tabular, Polaris, self-hosted) all All extras

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
import pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog
from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, load_data_to_iceberg

catalog = load_catalog("default")
data = pa.Table.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "signup_date": ["2023-01-01", "2023-01-02"]})

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", partition_col="day(signup_date)", schema_evolution=True)
load_data_to_iceberg(data, ("db", "users"), catalog, config=config)

The default write_mode is 'overwrite'. Calling a loader without config, or with a LoaderConfig that does not set write_mode, replaces all data in the table. Set write_mode="append" explicitly unless you mean to overwrite.

docs.title: Which function to use?
docs.text: Function Use when... Input format load_data_to_iceberg You have a single pa.Table in memory. pyarrow.Table load_batches_to_iceberg You have a generator/iterator of batches (memory efficient). Iterator of pyarrow.RecordBatch load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg You are reading from an Arrow IPC stream file/socket. File-like object or path register_parquet_files The data already exists as Parquet and should be referenced, not rewritten. Paths to Parquet files

docs.title: REST Catalog Setup
docs.text:
You can use REST Catalog via the built-in get_rest_catalog() helper, the RestCatalog constructor directly, or through a ~/.pyiceberg.yaml configuration file.

Option A: get_rest_catalog() helper (recommended)

from iceberg_loader import get_rest_catalog

catalog = get_rest_catalog(
    uri="https://api.tabular.io/ws",
    warehouse="s3://my-bucket/warehouse/",
    credential="your-oauth2-credential",
    s3_endpoint="https://s3.amazonaws.com",
    s3_region="us-east-1",
)

The helper also reads from environment variables — see help(get_rest_catalog) for all options.

Option B: Direct constructor

import os
from pyiceberg.catalog.rest import RestCatalog

# Only include optional properties that are actually set, so unset env vars
# don't pass None into RestCatalog.
optional_properties = {
    key: value
    for key, value in {
        "credential": os.environ.get("ICEBERG_CREDENTIAL"),  # OAuth2 credential; unset for a catalog without auth
        "s3.endpoint": os.environ.get("S3_ENDPOINT"),
        "s3.access-key-id": os.environ.get("S3_ACCESS_KEY"),
        "s3.secret-access-key": os.environ.get("S3_SECRET_KEY"),
        "s3.region": os.environ.get("S3_REGION"),
    }.items()
    if value is not None
}

catalog = RestCatalog(
    name="my-rest-catalog",
    uri=os.environ["ICEBERG_REST_URI"],          # e.g. https://api.tabular.io/ws
    warehouse=os.environ["ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE"],   # e.g. s3://my-bucket/warehouse/
    **optional_properties,
)

Prefer get_rest_catalog() (Option A) — it handles env-var resolution and omits unset properties for you.

Option C: pyiceberg.yaml + load_catalog()

# ~/.pyiceberg.yaml (see examples/pyiceberg.yaml.sample for a full annotated example)
catalog:
  my-rest-catalog:
    type: rest
    uri: https://api.tabular.io/ws
    warehouse: s3://my-bucket/warehouse/
    credential: your-oauth2-credential
    s3.endpoint: https://s3.amazonaws.com
    s3.region: us-east-1

from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

catalog = load_catalog("my-rest-catalog")

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
import pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog
from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, load_data_to_iceberg

catalog = load_catalog("default")

data = pa.Table.from_pydict({
    "id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "created_at": [1672531200000, 1672617600000, 1672704000000],
    "signup_date": ["2023-01-01", "2023-01-01", "2023-01-02"]
})

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", partition_col="day(signup_date)", schema_evolution=True)
result = load_data_to_iceberg(
    table_data=data,
    table_identifier=("my_db", "my_table"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=config,
)

print(result)
# {'rows_loaded': 3, 'write_mode': 'append', 'partition_col': 'day(signup_date)', ...}

docs.title: Preparing Data
docs.text:
These helpers convert Python dictionaries to Arrow data, including mixed fields:

from iceberg_loader.utils.arrow import create_arrow_table_from_data, create_record_batches_from_dicts

# 1. Convert list of dicts -> pa.Table
arrow_table = create_arrow_table_from_data(data_list)

# 2. Convert iterator of dicts -> Iterator[pa.RecordBatch]
batches = create_record_batches_from_dicts(data_generator(), batch_size=10000)

Alternatively, use standard PyArrow conversion: pa.Table.from_pylist(data).

The helpers serialize dicts and lists as JSON and convert other non-null values to strings too. For example, an integer id becomes an Arrow string. If you need to preserve scalar types, prepare a typed Arrow table with PyArrow instead.

The helpers sort columns by name, so a table they create gets alphabetical column order. Existing tables keep their own order.

docs.title: Idempotent Load (Replace Partition)
docs.text:
Replace data for a specific day without adding duplicate rows:

day_data = pa.Table.from_pydict({
    "id": [1, 2],
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob"],
    "signup_date": ["2023-01-01", "2023-01-01"],
})

config = LoaderConfig(
    write_mode="append",
    replace_filter="signup_date == '2023-01-01T00:00:00'",
    partition_col="day(signup_date)",
)

load_data_to_iceberg(table_data=day_data, table_identifier=("my_db", "my_table"), catalog=catalog, config=config)

The filter must cover every row you load: rows outside it are not deleted first, so they are duplicated on each rerun.

A string column partitioned with year/month/day/hour is stored as timestamp(us) when the loader creates the table, so the filter must compare it with a full timestamp literal ('2023-01-01T00:00:00'). A date-only literal such as '2023-01-01' raises ValueError: Invalid timestamp without zone. A column that is already date typed keeps its type, so filter it with a date literal ('2023-01-01').

The delete and the first commit run in one transaction; later commits of the same load are separate (see Commits and atomicity).

docs.title: Upsert (Merge Into)
docs.text:
Update matching rows and insert new ones using key columns. join_cols is required: tables created by the loader have no identifier fields, so PyIceberg cannot infer the keys.

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="upsert", join_cols=["id"])
load_data_to_iceberg(table_data=data, table_identifier=("my_db", "my_table"), catalog=catalog, config=config)

docs.title: Batch Loading
docs.text:
For large datasets, use load_batches_to_iceberg with an iterator of RecordBatches:

from iceberg_loader import load_batches_to_iceberg

def batch_generator():
    for i in range(10):
        yield some_record_batch

result = load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator=batch_generator(),
    table_identifier=("my_db", "large_table"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", commit_interval=100),
)

docs.title: Stream Loading (Arrow IPC)
docs.text:
Load data directly from an Apache Arrow IPC stream:

from iceberg_loader import load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg

result = load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg(
    stream_source="data.arrow",
    table_identifier=("my_db", "stream_table"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=LoaderConfig(write_mode="append"),
)

docs.title: Custom Settings
docs.text:
Set table properties for a new table:

custom_props = {
    'write.parquet.compression-codec': 'snappy',
    'history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep': 5,
}

config = LoaderConfig(table_properties=custom_props, write_mode="append")
load_data_to_iceberg(..., config=config)

table_properties apply only when the loader creates the table. Loading into an existing table never changes any of its properties: with the example above, a table created earlier with zstd keeps zstd. To change properties of an existing table, use PyIceberg directly (table.transaction().set_properties(...)).

docs.title: Override Default Table Properties Globally
docs.text:
Built-in defaults live in iceberg_loader.core.config.TABLE_PROPERTIES (format version, Parquet compression, commit retries). To tweak them, copy the dictionary, override keys, and pass into LoaderConfig:

from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog
from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, load_data_to_iceberg
from iceberg_loader.core.config import TABLE_PROPERTIES

catalog = load_catalog("default")

custom_properties = {**TABLE_PROPERTIES, "write.parquet.compression-codec": "gzip"}

config = LoaderConfig(
    write_mode="append",
    table_properties=custom_properties,
)

load_data_to_iceberg(table_data, ("default", "events"), catalog, config=config)

Because this copies format-version into your own table_properties, it counts as set explicitly: loading into an existing table of another version logs a warning (see below).

docs.title: Timestamp precision and format version
docs.text:
• Iceberg format v1/v2 stores timestamps in microseconds. Nanosecond input (pa.timestamp('ns')) is truncated to microseconds; when values actually lose precision, the loader logs a warning naming the column.
  • format-version in table_properties applies only when the loader creates a table. Loading into an existing table never changes its version; if you set format-version explicitly and it differs from the table's version, the loader logs a warning. The library default (format-version: 2) does not trigger it.
  • PyIceberg cannot write format v3 tables yet. Requesting format-version: 3 for a new table, or loading into an existing v3 table, raises NotImplementedError before anything is written.
  • A format-version that is not a whole number (e.g. 'v2' or 2.9) is ignored for existing tables, with a warning.

For timestamp columns, prefer partition transforms such as day(ts) or hour(ts), especially when using load_timestamp.

docs.title: Maintenance Helper
docs.text:
from iceberg_loader import expire_snapshots

table = catalog.load_table(("db", "users"))
expire_snapshots(table, keep_last=2)
  • keep_last (default 1) is meant to keep the N most recent snapshots; a negative value skips expiration.
  • older_than_ms (epoch milliseconds) expires snapshots older than that time instead; when set, keep_last is ignored.
  • Known issue: the cutoff is computed as a local naive datetime, which PyIceberg reads as UTC. On a host whose timezone is not UTC, both options are shifted by the UTC offset, so more or fewer snapshots than requested can be expired. keep_last=0 expires nothing. Run maintenance with TZ=UTC until this is fixed.
  • Errors during expiration (commit conflicts, I/O, invalid arguments) are logged as warnings and not raised.

docs.title: Registering Existing Parquet Files
docs.text:
If the data already exists as Parquet, register the files instead of reading and rewriting them:

from iceberg_loader import register_parquet_files

result = register_parquet_files(
    ["/data/events/part-0001.parquet", "/data/events/part-0002.parquet"],
    ("db", "events"),
    catalog,
)
# {'files_added': 2, 'rows_added': 1500, 'snapshot_id': 1234567890, 'table_location': '...'}
  • Metadata-only: the files are referenced by the table; they are not copied, converted, or moved. Their physical location must stay reachable by every reader for as long as the data is expected to be readable.
  • The table must already exist. Partitioned tables are supported: partition values are inferred from each file's Parquet statistics, so each file must stay within one partition and must have min/max statistics for the partition source columns. A file without them raises ValueError (its partition value would be NULL and filtered reads would skip its rows); PyIceberg rejects a file that spans more than one partition.
  • Footers are read through the table's FileIO (so catalog S3 credentials apply) and every file is validated before anything is committed: one bad file leaves no snapshot.
  • Missing nullable columns are allowed and read as NULL. An unknown column, a missing required column, or a required column stored as optional raises ValueError naming the file and column.
  • Files with embedded Parquet field IDs (PARQUET:field_id, written by Iceberg/Spark writers) raise ValueError: PyIceberg maps them by ID, not by name, so columns could be read swapped or as NULL. Load such data with load_data_to_iceberg instead.
  • Nanosecond timestamps raise ValueError unless the table column is a nanosecond timestamp.
  • Column type compatibility follows PyIceberg's promotion rules (for example int32 → int64); an incompatible type raises ValueError naming the file, column and both types. Nested and unmapped column types are left to PyIceberg's own validation.
  • check_duplicate_files=True (default) refuses files already referenced by the current snapshot. Paths are compared after normalization, so /data/a.parquet and file:///data/a.parquet count as the same file, both within one call and against the table. Passing False skips the table check, logs a warning, and can duplicate rows.
  • Paths must be absolute local paths or URIs (file://, s3://, …); they are stored in the table exactly as given. Relative paths raise ValueError.
  • Use this for migration. Use load_data_to_iceberg when the data is in memory, needs schema evolution, or needs a write mode such as overwrite or upsert.

docs.title: Incremental Loading with a Watermark
docs.text:
For append-only sources, read the high watermark from the destination, filter the source with > watermark, and load only the rows that arrived after the previous run:

from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, get_high_watermark, load_data_to_iceberg

table_id = ("db", "events")
# A missing table raises NoSuchTableError, so check for it on the first run.
watermark = get_high_watermark(table_id, "updated_at", catalog) if catalog.table_exists(table_id) else None
if watermark is None:  # first run or empty table: `> NULL` would match nothing
    new_rows = source.query("SELECT * FROM events")
else:
    new_rows = source.query("SELECT * FROM events WHERE updated_at > ?", [watermark])
load_data_to_iceberg(new_rows, table_id, catalog, LoaderConfig(write_mode="append"))

A timestamp column returns a naive datetime and a timestamptz column returns a UTC-aware one. Compare it with source values of the same kind: Python raises TypeError when comparing naive and aware datetimes.

get_high_watermark returns the maximum visible value of the column in its Python type, or None when the table has no rows or the column is all NULL (or NaN). Handle None explicitly: passing it to > ? filters out every source row, so the pipeline would never load anything. Persisting the watermark between runs is the orchestrator's job (an Airflow Variable/XCom, a database row, an object in S3, and so on); this helper never stores checkpoints.

Mode What it reads Cost Notes auto (default) Metadata when its preconditions hold, otherwise a scan Cheapest that is correct Silent fallback; the reason is logged at debug level metadata Maximum upper_bound in the data-file metadata Manifests only Top-level numeric/temporal columns, no delete files; raises ValueError otherwise scan The visible column, batch by batch, then max() Full column scan Works for every primitive type; accounts for position deletes (PyIceberg raises on equality deletes)

Correctness caveats:

  • Truncated string bounds: Iceberg truncates string/binary statistics, so metadata mode refuses those columns (ValueError suggesting mode="scan"). auto falls back to a scan.
  • Delete files: data-file bounds may include rows hidden by deletes, so metadata mode refuses tables with delete files. scan reads only visible rows.
  • NaN: ignored for float/double columns. A column with only NaN and NULL returns None from scan/auto; metadata refuses it because PyIceberg does not record NaN counts.
  • Equal timestamps: a late-arriving row whose timestamp is equal to or below the watermark is not re-read by > watermark. Use >= with a de-duplicating strategy if that can happen.

Nested, dotted, and unknown column names raise ValueError naming the available top-level columns.

docs.title: Adding Load Timestamp
docs.text:
Set load_timestamp to add a timestamp column (by default, _load_dttm) to every row. You can use it for audit trails or partitioning by load time.

from datetime import datetime

# Will add column '_load_dttm' with current time and partition by hour
config = LoaderConfig(
    write_mode="append",
    load_timestamp=datetime.now(),
    partition_col="hour(_load_dttm)",
)

# You can also customize the column name and day-transform it
config_custom = LoaderConfig(
    write_mode="append",
    load_timestamp=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    load_ts_col="etl_ts",
    partition_col="day(etl_ts)",
)

docs.title: Reusing a Loader (IcebergLoader)
docs.text:
The load_*_to_iceberg functions create a new IcebergLoader on every call. To share settings across calls, create one yourself:

from iceberg_loader import IcebergLoader, LoaderConfig

loader = IcebergLoader(
    catalog,
    table_properties={"write.parquet.compression-codec": "snappy"},
    default_config=LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", schema_evolution=True),
)

loader.load_data(arrow_table, ("db", "users"))                     # uses default_config
loader.load_data_batches(batches, ("db", "events"))                 # uses default_config
loader.load_ipc_stream("data.arrow", ("db", "stream_table"))
loader.load_data(arrow_table, ("db", "users"), config=LoaderConfig(write_mode="overwrite"))
  • A per-call config replaces default_config entirely; fields are not merged. In the last call above, schema_evolution is back to False.
  • Table properties for a new table are merged in this order, later wins: TABLE_PROPERTIES → IcebergLoader(table_properties=...) → LoaderConfig.table_properties.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
The library logs to the iceberg_loader logger and, like other libraries, prints nothing on its own: records propagate to your application's logging setup, which controls format and level. Without any configuration, Python shows only warnings and errors.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)                    # library INFO messages in your format
logging.getLogger("iceberg_loader").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)  # also the METRIC: load_completed line

If you want the library's own stderr handler instead (TEXT or JSON), call configure_logging before loading. It attaches that handler and sets propagate=False, so messages no longer reach your root handlers:

from iceberg_loader.services.logging import configure_logging

configure_logging(level="WARNING", log_format="JSON")

In TEXT format the level name is colored when stderr is a terminal; set NO_COLOR=1 to turn that off. Redirected output (files, CI logs) stays plain.

docs.title: Commits and atomicity
docs.text:
• Each commit covers up to commit_interval batches. commit_interval=0 (the default) and 1 both mean one commit per batch, not one transaction for the whole load.
  • load_data_to_iceberg splits a pa.Table into its record batches (one per chunk), so a multi-chunk table is also written in several commits.
  • A load that fails midway leaves the commits that already succeeded. With replace_filter, the delete happens in the first commit only, so a failed load can leave the old rows deleted and the new rows partially written. With write_mode="overwrite", the table is overwritten by the first commit and appended to by the rest.
  • To write a load in a single commit, set commit_interval to at least the number of batches (for a pa.Table, len(table.to_batches()), or call table.combine_chunks() first to get a single batch).

docs.title: Write modes
docs.text:
• The default write_mode is 'overwrite'. See the note in Quickstart.
  • replace_filter works with 'append' and 'overwrite': both delete matching rows and append (delete-then-append), so 'overwrite' with a filter does not overwrite the whole table.
  • replace_filter must match every row being loaded; rows outside the filter are appended again on each rerun.
  • An empty input with a known schema (an empty pa.Table, an IPC stream or RecordBatchReader without batches) still runs the write: it creates the table if needed, 'overwrite' clears the table, and replace_filter deletes the matching rows. A plain iterator that yields no batches has no schema: nothing is written, an existing table is left unchanged, and a warning is logged.
  • replace_filter cannot be combined with write_mode='upsert' (rejected by LoaderConfig).
  • Upsert needs join_cols (see Upsert).

docs.title: Schema and types
docs.text:
• schema_evolution=False (the default): columns that are not in the table are dropped silently. Columns missing from the data are written as NULL.
  • Batches in one commit may have different schemas (column order, extra or missing columns): each batch is cast to the table schema.
  • schema_evolution=True adds new top-level columns only. It does not change existing column types.
  • Data is cast to the table's column types. If a safe cast fails for any value in a column, the whole column of that commit is written as NULL, and a warning naming the column is logged.
  • Lossy casts that PyArrow can perform unsafely go through without a warning: floats are truncated to integers (1.9 → 1), and integer overflow wraps (int64 → int32). The only lossy cast that warns is timestamp precision loss (e.g. ns → us).
  • Nested Arrow types (struct, list, map) are not supported: creating or evolving a table with them raises ValueError: Unsupported PyArrow type. Use create_arrow_table_from_data to serialize nested values as JSON strings.

docs.title: Partitioning
docs.text:
• partition_col accepts one field: a column name or a transform (year, month, day, hour, bucket(N, col), truncate(N, col)).
  • The partition spec is set only when the loader creates the table. Changing partition_col later does not repartition an existing table.
  • A string column used with year/month/day/hour is promoted to timestamp(us) at table creation; filter it with timestamp literals (see Idempotent Load).
  • If partition_col names a column that is not in the data, the table is created without partitions and only a warning is logged.
  • A transform that does not fit the column type (for example, day(...) on an integer column) fails the load with a ValidationError.
  • Identity partitioning on the load timestamp column is rejected; use day(...) or hour(...).

docs.title: Table properties
docs.text: • All table_properties, including format-version, apply only when the loader creates the table (see Custom Settings).

docs.title: LoaderConfig Reference
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description write_mode 'append' | 'overwrite' | 'upsert' 'overwrite' Data write mode. The default overwrites the table; set 'append' explicitly to add data partition_col str \| None None Partition column or transform (e.g., month(ts), bucket(16,id)); one field, applied only when the table is created; prefer day/hour on timestamps replace_filter str \| None None SQL-style filter for idempotent loads (delete-then-append) schema_evolution bool False Auto-add new columns; when False, unknown columns are dropped commit_interval int 0 Commit every N batches; 0 and 1 both commit after every batch join_cols list[str] \| None None Merge keys for upsert (required for 'upsert') table_properties dict \| None None Custom Iceberg table properties; applied only when the loader creates the table load_timestamp datetime \| None None If set, adds a load_ts_col column (default _load_dttm) with this value load_ts_col str '_load_dttm' Name of the load timestamp column

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Pass write options only through LoaderConfig; the table above lists its fields.

docs.title: load_data_to_iceberg()
docs.text:
Loads a pa.Table held in memory. The table is written batch by batch (one batch per chunk).

def load_data_to_iceberg(
    table_data: pa.Table,
    table_identifier: tuple[str, str],
    catalog: Catalog,
    config: LoaderConfig | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]

docs.title: load_batches_to_iceberg()
docs.text:
Loads a stream of batches into an Iceberg table.

def load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator: Iterator[pa.RecordBatch] | pa.RecordBatchReader,
    table_identifier: tuple[str, str],
    catalog: Catalog,
    config: LoaderConfig | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]

docs.title: load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg()
docs.text:
Reads an Arrow IPC stream (path, file-like object, or pa.NativeFile) and loads its batches.

def load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg(
    stream_source: str | BinaryIO | pa.NativeFile,
    table_identifier: tuple[str, str],
    catalog: Catalog,
    config: LoaderConfig | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]

docs.title: IcebergLoader
docs.text:
class IcebergLoader:
    def __init__(
        self,
        catalog: Catalog,
        table_properties: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        default_config: LoaderConfig | None = None,
    ): ...

    def load_data(self, table_data, table_identifier, config=None) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
    def load_data_batches(self, batch_iterator, table_identifier, config=None) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
    def load_ipc_stream(self, stream_source, table_identifier, config=None) -> dict[str, Any]: ...

See Reusing a Loader for how default_config and table_properties combine.

docs.title: get_rest_catalog()
docs.text:
def get_rest_catalog(
    name: str = "rest-catalog",
    *,
    uri: str | None = None,              # env: ICEBERG_REST_URI (required)
    warehouse: str | None = None,        # env: ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE
    credential: str | None = None,       # env: ICEBERG_CREDENTIAL
    s3_endpoint: str | None = None,      # env: S3_ENDPOINT
    s3_access_key: str | None = None,    # env: S3_ACCESS_KEY
    s3_secret_key: str | None = None,    # env: S3_SECRET_KEY
    s3_region: str | None = None,        # env: S3_REGION
    s3_path_style: bool = False,
    extra_properties: dict[str, str] | None = None,
) -> RestCatalog

Explicit arguments win over environment variables. Path-style S3 access is enabled automatically when an S3 endpoint is set. extra_properties are applied last and override every other key. Raises ValueError when no URI is given.

docs.title: register_parquet_files()
docs.text:
Registers existing Parquet files in an existing Iceberg table without rewriting them.

def register_parquet_files(
    file_paths: Sequence[str],
    table_identifier: tuple[str, str],
    catalog: Catalog,
    *,
    snapshot_properties: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    check_duplicate_files: bool = True,
) -> dict[str, Any]

Returns {'files_added': int, 'rows_added': int, 'snapshot_id': int | str, 'table_location': str}. snapshot_id is the string 'none' when there is no snapshot. See Registering Existing Parquet Files.

docs.title: get_high_watermark()
docs.text:
Returns the maximum visible value of column, for filtering the source of an incremental load.

def get_high_watermark(
    table_identifier: tuple[str, str],
    column: str,
    catalog: Catalog,
    *,
    mode: Literal["auto", "metadata", "scan"] = "auto",
) -> Any

The value is returned in the column's Python type, or None when the table has no rows or the column is all NULL. Raises NoSuchTableError when the table does not exist. metadata raises ValueError when the column type or the table state makes the file bounds untrustworthy; auto falls back to a scan in those cases. See Incremental Loading with a Watermark for the trade-offs.

docs.title: Return value of the load functions
docs.text:
{
    'rows_loaded': int,
    'batches_processed': int,
    'write_mode': str,
    'partition_col': str,        # the string 'none' when not set
    'table_location': str,       # the string 'none' when the table does not exist after the load
    'snapshot_id': int | str,    # the string 'none' when there is no snapshot
    'new_table_created': bool,   # True only when this load created the table
    'conform_ms': float,         # conforming batches: table load/create, schema evolution commits, casts
    'write_ms': float,           # writing and committing batches
    'total_ms': float,           # the whole load, excluding config resolution
    'casts_applied': int,        # columns successfully cast (including lossy)
    'casts_lossy': int,          # subset of applied that only succeeded in unsafe mode (truncated or wrapped values)
    'casts_failed': int,         # columns with a failed cast, filled with NULLs
}

Note that the "empty" values are the string 'none', not None.

  • Timings: total_ms - conform_ms - write_ms is mostly the time spent reading the input (a generator, an IPC stream) plus the final snapshot lookup, so a slow source shows up there, not in write_ms.
  • Cast counters count distinct columns per load, not rows, batches, or buffers: a column cast in every batch counts once, regardless of commit_interval, schema_evolution, or how the input is chunked. casts_lossy covers timestamp precision loss, float→int truncation, and integer overflow (wrapped values). A column whose batches behaved differently can be counted in both casts_applied and casts_failed.

Each successful load emits one METRIC: load_completed debug log with the same timing and cast fields. A load that raises emits no metric.

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
Basic stream loading:

def generate_batches():
    for i in range(100):
        data = {"id": [i], "value": [f"row_{i}"]}
        yield pa.RecordBatch.from_pydict(data)

result = load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator=generate_batches(),
    table_identifier=("db", "table"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=LoaderConfig(write_mode="append")
)

With commits for memory management:

result = load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator=large_batch_stream,
    table_identifier=("db", "large_table"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=LoaderConfig(
        write_mode="append",
        commit_interval=50,
        schema_evolution=True
    )
)

Idempotent partition loading:

result = load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator=daily_batches,  # event_date is a string column, e.g. "2023-12-09"
    table_identifier=("db", "events"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=LoaderConfig(
        write_mode="append",
        replace_filter="event_date == '2023-12-09T00:00:00'",
        partition_col="day(event_date)"
    )
)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
See Examples for scripts covering streaming, upserts, schema evolution, and mixed JSON fields.

For how the package is put together, see Architecture.

docs.title: Public API & versioning
docs.text:
• Semantic Versioning from 0.1.x: MINOR = new compatible features, PATCH = fixes, MAJOR = breaking changes. Breaking changes to documented APIs are noted in RELEASE.md.
  • Public API: LoaderConfig, IcebergLoader, load_data_to_iceberg, load_batches_to_iceberg, load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg, register_parquet_files, get_high_watermark, get_rest_catalog, expire_snapshots. Data conversion helpers live in iceberg_loader.utils.arrow. Other modules are internal.
  • Pass loading options via LoaderConfig; avoid legacy positional arguments.
  • Prefer partition transforms for timestamps (day(ts), hour(ts), day(_load_dttm)) to avoid unbounded partition counts.
  • LoaderConfig validates partition expressions and forbids unsafe mixes (e.g., replace_filter with upsert, identity partition on _load_dttm).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: How iceberg-loader moves Arrow data through table setup, schema handling, and write strategies.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Module Role Public API iceberg_loader/__init__.py Re-exports LoaderConfig, IcebergLoader, the load_*_to_iceberg functions, register_parquet_files, get_high_watermark, get_rest_catalog, expire_snapshots, and the module-level logger. load_*_to_iceberg core/loader.py Thin wrappers: each call builds a new IcebergLoader with the given config and delegates to it. IcebergLoader core/loader.py Orchestrator. Resolves the effective config and table properties, buffers batches up to commit_interval, passes each buffer to BatchConformer, then writes it with a WriteStrategy. BatchConformer core/conform.py One instance per load. Owns the target table: loads or creates it, appends the load timestamp column, evolves the schema, and casts each buffer to the table schema. SchemaManager core/schema.py Table lifecycle: ensure_table_exists() (create with partition spec and properties, or load and check the format version), evolve_schema_if_needed() (add top-level columns), Arrow↔Iceberg schema conversion. WriteStrategy core/strategies.py AppendStrategy, OverwriteStrategy (overwrite on the first commit, append after), IdempotentStrategy (delete by replace_filter in the first commit, then append), UpsertStrategy (PyIceberg table.upsert). get_write_strategy() picks one. LoaderConfig core/config.py Frozen Pydantic model with all load options. Validates partition expressions and rejects unsafe combinations. TABLE_PROPERTIES holds the default table properties. register_parquet_files core/register.py Validates existing Parquet footers (schema, field IDs, partition statistics, paths) and references the files with Table.add_files() in one snapshot. Partitioning core/partitioning.py Parses day(ts), bucket(16, id), etc. into PyIceberg transforms. Arrow utilities utils/arrow.py create_arrow_table_from_data / create_record_batches_from_dicts (dicts → Arrow, nested values → JSON strings) and convert_table_types (cast to a target schema; a column whose safe cast fails becomes all NULL, with a warning). Type mappings utils/types.py TypeRegistry: Arrow↔Iceberg type mapping, extensible with register_custom_mapping(). get_rest_catalog catalog.py Builds a PyIceberg RestCatalog from arguments or environment variables. Logging services/logging.py Module-level logger proxy over the iceberg_loader logger; configure_logging() sets level and TEXT/JSON format. Maintenance services/maintenance.py SnapshotMaintenance and expire_snapshots(). Compatibility shim iceberg_loader/iceberg_loader.py Keeps from iceberg_loader.iceberg_loader import ... working: aliases IcebergLoader and repeats the three wrapper functions.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
load_data_to_iceberg(pa.Table)            ──► IcebergLoader.load_data()        ── table.to_batches() ──┐
load_batches_to_iceberg(Iterator[Batch])  ──► IcebergLoader.load_data_batches()                        ├─► load_data_batches()
load_ipc_stream_to_iceberg(path/stream)   ──► IcebergLoader.load_ipc_stream()  ── pa.ipc.open_stream() ┘
register_parquet_files(paths)             ──► core/register.py ── footer schema check ── Table.add_files()

load_data_batches()
  ├─ resolve config (per-call config replaces default_config) and table properties
  ├─ strategy = get_write_strategy(write_mode, replace_filter, join_cols)
  ├─ conformer = BatchConformer(...)
  └─ for buffer in _buffered(batches, max(1, commit_interval)):     # one commit per buffer
        data = conformer.conform(buffer)
        strategy.write(conformer.table, data, is_first_write)

BatchConformer.conform(buffer):

buffer of RecordBatches
  ├─ without schema_evolution: concat the buffer (mixed schemas → pa.ArrowInvalid, before any table exists)
  ├─ add load timestamp column (if load_timestamp is set)
  ├─ first call only: SchemaManager.ensure_table_exists()
  │     new table: promote string partition source to timestamp(us) for time transforms,
  │                build partition spec, apply table properties
  │     existing table: properties and partition spec are left as they are
  ├─ evolve: add the load timestamp column; with schema_evolution, add new columns from every distinct batch schema;
  │     all in one schema commit per buffer, so a buffer that fails conversion adds no columns
  └─ convert_table_types() to the table's Arrow schema
        unknown columns dropped, missing columns NULL, a column with a failed safe cast all NULL + warning,
        timestamp precision loss (e.g. ns → us) warned

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The scripts in examples/ cover loading, catalog setup, and maintenance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You need a running Iceberg catalog and MinIO/S3. The bundled docker-compose.yml starts a local stack (run from the examples/ directory):

cd examples
docker compose up -d

The bundled stack includes:

  • MinIO (S3) at http://localhost:9000 (console http://localhost:9001, minio/minio123)
  • Hive Metastore at thrift://localhost:9083
  • Trino at http://localhost:8080, with two catalogs: iceberg reads the Hive Metastore, iceberg_rest reads Polaris
  • Apache Polaris REST Catalog at http://localhost:8181/api/catalog (root/root)

minio/minio is no longer published on Docker Hub, so the stack uses coollabsio/minio, a rebuild of the official release. Use it (or any other S3-compatible store) in your own compose file too.

To query a table loaded through Polaris, prefix it with the REST catalog: SELECT * FROM iceberg_rest."default".my_table. The Trino side of that is trino-etc/catalog/iceberg_rest.properties.

Then run examples from the same examples/ directory (see commands below). With uv you can prefix any command as uv run python <script.py>.

docs.title: Loading Data in Batches
docs.text:
Load data from an iterator of RecordBatches:

import pyarrow as pa
from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, load_batches_to_iceberg

def generate_batches():
    for i in range(10):
        data = {
            'id': list(range(i * 100, (i + 1) * 100)),
            'name': [f'Item_{j}' for j in range(100)],
        }
        yield pa.RecordBatch.from_pydict(data)

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", schema_evolution=True)
result = load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator=generate_batches(),
    table_identifier=("db", "items"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=config,
)

docs.title: Commit Interval (Streaming)
docs.text:
Use commit_interval to flush batches periodically during long-running streams:

from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, load_batches_to_iceberg

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", commit_interval=100)
result = load_batches_to_iceberg(
    batch_iterator=my_batch_generator(),
    table_identifier=("db", "events"),
    catalog=catalog,
    config=config,
)

docs.title: Upsert (Merge)
docs.text:
Perform merge operations (update existing, insert new) based on key columns:

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="upsert", join_cols=["id"])
load_data_to_iceberg(data, ("db", "users"), catalog, config=config)

docs.title: Dynamic Configuration (Multi-table Load)
docs.text:
Choose a LoaderConfig for each table in a loop:

# Define configurations
config_overwrite = LoaderConfig(write_mode='overwrite', schema_evolution=True)
config_upsert = LoaderConfig(write_mode='upsert', join_cols=['id'], schema_evolution=True)

# Map endpoints/tables to specific configs
endpoint_configs = {
    'customers': config_overwrite,
    'orders': config_upsert,
}

for endpoint in endpoints:
    # Use specific config or default to append
    current_config = endpoint_configs.get(endpoint, LoaderConfig(write_mode='append'))

    load_data_to_iceberg(
        table_data=data,
        table_identifier=('default', endpoint),
        catalog=catalog,
        config=current_config
    )

docs.title: Messy JSON
docs.text:
For mixed or nested values that PyArrow cannot convert directly, iceberg-loader serializes dicts and lists as JSON strings:

from iceberg_loader import LoaderConfig, load_data_to_iceberg
from iceberg_loader.utils.arrow import create_arrow_table_from_data

data = [
    {"id": 1, "complex_field": {"a": 1, "b": "nested"}},
    {"id": 2, "complex_field": {"a": 2, "b": "another", "c": [1, 2]}},
    {"id": 3, "complex_field": [1, 2, 3]},
]

arrow_table = create_arrow_table_from_data(data)

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="append")
load_data_to_iceberg(arrow_table, ("db", "events"), catalog, config=config)

docs.title: Schema Evolution
docs.text:
Set schema_evolution=True to add columns found in incoming data:

config = LoaderConfig(write_mode="append", schema_evolution=True)
load_data_to_iceberg(data_with_new_columns, ("db", "table"), catalog, config=config)

docs.title: Partitioning
docs.text:
Create partitioned tables with transform expressions:

from datetime import datetime

config = LoaderConfig(
    write_mode="append",
    partition_col="month(event_date)",  # or day(), year(), bucket(16, id), etc.
)
load_data_to_iceberg(data, ("db", "events"), catalog, config=config)

ingestion_config = LoaderConfig(
    write_mode="append",
    load_timestamp=datetime.now(),
    partition_col="hour(_load_dttm)",
)
